name: Socks, Drawers & Guarantees
lesson: If more objects than boxes are placed into boxes, at least one box receives two objects. The boxes can represent colours, remainders, months or other categories.
A guarantee must survive the most awkward possible outcome. First find the greatest number of choices that could still avoid the desired event, then add one.
For harder questions, invent useful groups. Pairing numbers or dividing a space into regions can turn a large problem into a small counting argument.

problems.q: Socks come in four colours, with plenty of each colour. You draw socks without looking. How many guarantee two socks of the same colour?
problems.hint: You could draw one of each colour first.
problems.solution: Four socks might all have different colours. The fifth must match one of the four colours already drawn.

problems.q: How many people guarantee that at least two have birthdays in the same month?
problems.solution: Twelve people could occupy twelve different months. A thirteenth person must share a month with someone.

problems.q: Ten balls are placed into three boxes. What is the smallest number of balls that at least one box must contain?
problems.hint: Three balls in every box accounts for only 9 balls.
problems.solution: If each box held at most 3 balls, there would be at most 9. Thus some box has at least 4. A $4,3,3$ distribution shows 4 is the best guarantee.

problems.q: Badges come in five colours, with plenty of each. How many draws guarantee three badges of one colour?
problems.hint: You could draw two of each colour without having three alike.
problems.solution: Ten draws can give two of each colour. The next draw creates a group of at least three, so 11 suffice.

problems.q: Thirty-one books are placed on six shelves. At least one shelf must contain how many books? Give the strongest guarantee.
problems.hint: What if every shelf held at most five books?
problems.solution: Six shelves with at most five books each hold at most 30 books. Therefore some shelf has at least 6. A distribution $6,5,5,5,5,5$ shows this is sharp.

problems.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are drawn without replacement. How many draws guarantee an even number?
problems.hint: All the odd-numbered cards could come first.
problems.solution: There are five odd cards. The sixth draw must be even.

problems.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are drawn without replacement. How many draws guarantee two cards whose numbers add to 11?
problems.hint: Group the cards into pairs with sum 11.
problems.solution: The five pairs are $(1,10),(2,9),(3,8),(4,7),(5,6)$. Five draws can take one from each pair; six draws must complete a pair.

problems.q: A bag has four red, four green and four gold counters. How many draws without replacement guarantee at least one counter of every colour?
problems.hint: You might draw all the counters of two colours first.
problems.solution: Eight draws can still omit a colour. Only eight counters belong to the other two colours, so the ninth must supply the missing colour.

problems.q: Seven integers are chosen. Must two leave the same remainder when divided by 6?
problems.hint: Division by 6 has six possible remainders.
problems.solution: The remainders are $0,1,2,3,4,5$. Seven integers in six remainder categories must share a category.

problems.q: What is the largest number of cards you can choose from cards numbered 1 to 9 without choosing two consecutive numbers?
problems.solution: At most one card can be taken from each of the four pairs, plus card 9, so at most 5. Choosing $1,3,5,7,9$ achieves 5.

problems.q: A drawer has five red, five green and five gold socks. How many draws guarantee two disjoint matching pairs? The pairs may have the same colour.
problems.hint: With at most one matching pair, how many socks could each colour contribute?
problems.solution: To have at most one pair, one colour can contribute at most 3 socks and the others at most 1 each: at most 5 total. Six socks therefore guarantee two pairs. The distribution $3,1,1$ shows five do not suffice.

problems.q: How many whole numbers guarantee two whose difference is divisible by 16?
problems.solution: There are 16 possible remainders. Among 17 numbers, two share a remainder, so their difference is divisible by 16. Sixteen numbers, such as 0 through 15, need not contain such a pair.
